scenario: Save every line of /usr/share/dict/words that contains "ich" into /root/lines, in the original order. Which command does it?

options.note: find matches file names, not lines.

explanation: grep prints matching lines in the order they appear in the file, and > writes them to /root/lines. Adding sort would reorder them and -c would write a count instead of the lines. Read the task for output file, order and case rules.

scenario: Find every regular file owned by user harry and copy each one, keeping its attributes, into /root/found. Which command does it?

options.note: Misses files owned by harry elsewhere and copies files he doesn't own.

explanation: find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/found/ \; locates every regular file owned by harry and copies each with attributes preserved; create /root/found first. Add 2>/dev/null to hide permission noise.

scenario: Which find expression matches files larger than 30 MiB and smaller than 50 MiB?
explanation: find -size +30M -size -50M matches files strictly between those sizes (M is mebibytes); two -size tests are ANDed. The -size 30M-50M and -size >30M forms aren't valid, and -mtime tests age, not size.

scenario: Create a gzip-compressed archive /root/etc.tar.gz of /etc. Which command is correct?
explanation: tar -czf creates (c) a gzip (z) archive into the file (f). The -x option extracts, and -j makes bzip2 (not gzip). Use -cJf for xz.

scenario: Which command creates a symbolic link /root/logs that points to /var/log?

options.note: Hard links to directories aren't allowed.
Arguments are target, then link name.
cp -s creates symlinks only for files, and isn't the standard method.

explanation: ln -s TARGET LINK_NAME makes a symbolic link, so ln -s /var/log /root/logs creates /root/logs pointing to /var/log. Without -s you get a hard link, which can't point to a directory or cross file systems; reversing the arguments inverts the link.

scenario: Which command switches to user natasha with her login environment?

options.note: sudo runs a command; natasha isn't a command.

explanation: su - natasha starts a login shell with natasha's environment, whereas su without the dash keeps your own environment. sudo -i -u natasha does the same if sudoers allows it.

refs.title: Sudo Manual: Execute commands as another user

scenario: In ls -l output, what does drwxrws--- for /shared/sales indicate?

options.text: A directory with the SGID bit set: new files inherit its group

options.note: s in the group position is SGID.
That's t in the others position.

explanation: drwxrws--- is a directory with the SGID bit (s in the group execute position): new files inherit the directory's group. Mode 2770 sets it; SUID would show an s in the owner field and the sticky bit a t in the last.

scenario: Set /shared/docs so the owner and the group have full access, others none, and new files inherit the group. Which mode?

options.note: Sets the sticky bit, not SGID.
SUID has no effect on directories.

explanation: The leading digit holds the special bits (4 SUID, 2 SGID, 1 sticky), so 2770 gives owner and group full access, others none, and group inheritance on new files. 0770 has no SGID and 1770 is the sticky bit.

scenario: Which command shows the options of the useradd command in the documentation installed on the system?
explanation: The exam has no internet, so use installed documentation: man useradd (or useradd --help), man -k to search, info, and /usr/share/doc. help covers only shell builtins.

scenario: Which redirection appends both standard output and errors of a command to /root/out.log?
explanation: command >> file 2>&1 appends stdout to the file and then points stderr (2) at the same place. Order matters: 2>&1 must come after the file redirection, and a single > would overwrite rather than append.

scenario: Which command searches /etc for files containing "PermitRootLogin" and shows line numbers?
explanation: grep -rn PermitRootLogin /etc searches recursively (-r) and shows line numbers (-n). find -name matches file names, not contents, and -l prints only file names.

scenario: Which regular expression with grep -E matches lines beginning with "#" or ";" (comments)?

options.note: Matches at the end of the line.

explanation: With grep -E, ^[#;] matches lines whose first character is # or ;. Combine with -v and ^$ to show only active configuration lines: grep -Ev '^[#;]|^$' file.

scenario: Which command copies /root/report.txt to /tmp on server2 securely?

options.note: FTP is insecure and not installed.

explanation: scp copies files over SSH, so credentials and data are encrypted: scp /root/report.txt root@server2:/tmp/. rsync -e ssh and sftp work too, but cp can't reach another host and ftp is clear text.

scenario: Which command shows the permissions in octal, owner, and size of /etc/shadow?

options.note: Omits the group, and doesn't show octal.

explanation: stat shows octal permissions, owner, group and size; stat -c '%a %U %G' prints just mode, user and group. file reports content type, not permissions.

scenario: In vim, how do you replace every "http" with "https" in the whole file?

options.note: Only the first match on the current line.

explanation: In vim, :%s/http/https/g runs a substitution over every line (%) and replaces all matches per line (g). Without % only the current line changes, and without g only the first match per line.

scenario: Which command shows the 10 most recent lines of /var/log/messages and keeps showing new ones?
explanation: tail -f shows the last 10 lines and keeps printing new ones as they are added. head shows the beginning of a file, and journalctl -f follows the journal instead.

scenario: Which line should start a Bash script so it runs with Bash regardless of the user's shell?
explanation: The shebang #!/bin/bash on the first line tells the kernel which interpreter runs the script; make it executable with chmod +x and run it as ./script.sh. Without it the user's current shell interprets the file.

scenario: In a script, which variable holds the number of arguments passed?
explanation: $# holds the number of arguments. "$@" expands each argument as a separate word, $0 is the script name and $? is the last exit status.

scenario: Which construct runs a block only if the script received no arguments?

options.note: Loops and uses the wrong test.

explanation: if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then ... fi tests that no arguments were passed, typically printing usage and exiting nonzero. while and case are not conditional blocks for this.

scenario: Which loop prints each user name listed in /root/users.txt, one per line?

options.text: for u in $(cat /root/users.txt); do echo "$u"; done
for u in /root/users.txt; do echo $u; done
options.note: Loops once over the file name.

explanation: for u in $(cat /root/users.txt); do echo "$u"; done iterates over each word in the file. While read -r is safer for lines with spaces; looping over the path itself iterates once over the file name.

scenario: What does this script print if run as ./greet.sh alice bob? echo "Hello $2"
explanation: $1 is alice and $2 is bob, so echo "Hello $2" prints 'Hello bob'. Positional parameters beyond nine need braces, such as ${10}.

scenario: Which test checks that $1 is an existing directory?
explanation: [ -d "$1" ] is true when $1 is an existing directory; -f tests a regular file, -x executable and -z an empty string. Quote the variable so spaces don't break the test.

scenario: How does a script capture the hostname into a variable?

options.note: Spaces make Bash run "host" as a command.

explanation: host=$(hostname) uses command substitution to store the command's output in a variable. host=hostname stores the literal word, and spaces around = are not allowed.

scenario: Which script line exits with status 2 and an error message if /etc/app.conf is missing?
explanation: [ -f file ] || { echo "missing config" >&2; exit 2; } runs the right side only if the test fails, sending the message to stderr (>&2) and exiting with status 2. Using && would exit when the file exists.

scenario: Which loop counts from 1 to 5?

options.text: for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done
for i in 1-5; do echo $i; done

explanation: for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done uses brace expansion to count 1 through 5; a C-style loop for ((i=1; i<=5; i++)) also works, as does seq 1 5. 1-5 is just a string, and i<5 would stop at 4.

scenario: A script must print each line of command output that contains "error" with a prefix. Which pipeline fits?

options.text: journalctl -b | grep -i error | while read -r line; do echo "ALERT: $line"; done

options.note: Writes to a file named grep.

explanation: Piping into while read -r line handles output one line at a time, so journalctl -b | grep -i error | while read -r line; do echo "ALERT: $line"; done prefixes each match. Redirecting to a file named grep doesn't filter.

scenario: Which command makes the system boot to a text console by default?

options.note: Switches now but doesn't change the default.

explanation: systemctl set-default multi-user.target makes the system boot to a text console by default; graphical.target is the GUI default. isolate only switches the running system, and get-default shows the current setting.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: How do you boot once into rescue mode from the GRUB menu?

options.text: Press e on the entry and add systemd.unit=rescue.target to the linux line, then press Ctrl+X
Type rescue at the login prompt
Run systemctl rescue from another host

explanation: At GRUB press e, append systemd.unit=rescue.target to the linux line and press Ctrl+X to boot once into rescue mode. Changes made there last for that boot only; emergency.target is more minimal.

refs.title: Managing, monitoring, and updating the kernel - RHEL 9

scenario: You must reset a forgotten root password on RHEL. After adding rd.break (or init=/bin/bash) at GRUB, what is the key extra step before rebooting?

options.text: Ensure SELinux relabels or restore the shadow file context (touch /.autorelabel or restorecon /etc/shadow)

explanation: After resetting root's password from the initramfs shell (rd.break), you must trigger an SELinux relabel (touch /.autorelabel) or restore the shadow file context, otherwise logins can fail. Remount /sysroot read-write and chroot to run passwd.

scenario: Which command reboots the system immediately?
explanation: systemctl reboot reboots immediately. shutdown -r +5 schedules a reboot later, and systemctl poweroff powers off instead.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: Which command shows the processes using the most memory, sorted?
explanation: ps aux --sort=-%mem | head lists processes by memory use, highest first (the minus sign), keeping the top entries. In top, M sorts by memory and P by CPU.

scenario: Which command starts /usr/local/bin/batch.sh with a nice value of 15?
explanation: nice -n 15 command starts a new process at nice 15 (lower priority); renice changes one already running. Higher nice values mean lower priority.

scenario: A process named cpuhog uses all CPU. Which command ends every process with that name?

options.note: kill needs a PID unless using job specs.
Works only if it's a service unit.

explanation: pkill cpuhog (or killall) ends every process with that name; pgrep -l lists the PIDs first. kill needs PIDs, not names, and systemctl stop only works for services.

scenario: Which command applies the tuned profile recommended for the system?
explanation: tuned-adm profile $(tuned-adm recommend) applies the recommended profile; tuned-adm active shows the current one. The tuned service must be enabled and running.

refs.title: Managing, monitoring, and updating the kernel - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command shows journal messages with priority err or higher from the current boot?
explanation: journalctl -b -p err shows messages of priority err and higher from the current boot. Other filters include --since, -u unit and -o verbose.

scenario: How do you make the systemd journal persist across reboots?

options.text: Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (or create /var/log/journal) and restart systemd-journald

options.note: rsyslog writes text logs, but the journal stays volatile.

explanation: Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (or create /var/log/journal) and restart systemd-journald so logs survive reboots; then journalctl -b -1 shows the previous boot.

scenario: Which command starts the httpd service now and at every boot?

options.note: Starts only at the next boot.

explanation: systemctl enable --now httpd starts the service immediately and at every boot. Doing only start leaves it off after reboot, and only enable doesn't start it now.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: Which command securely copies a directory tree /var/www to server2, preserving permissions?

options.note: Needs -r and doesn't preserve everything by default.

explanation: rsync -av /var/www/ server2:/var/www/ copies recursively over SSH, preserving permissions and times, and only transfers changes. The trailing slash copies the contents. scp of a directory needs -r and doesn't preserve as much.

scenario: Which command lists all running services?
explanation: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running lists running services. list-unit-files shows enabled or disabled state instead.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: In top, a process shows NI 19. What does that mean?

options.text: It has the lowest scheduling priority

explanation: NI 19 is the nice value: the lowest scheduling priority. Regular users can only raise the nice value of their own processes.

scenario: Which command shows boot-time messages from the previous boot?
explanation: journalctl -b -1 shows messages from the previous boot, which requires a persistent journal. -b 0 is the current boot.

scenario: Which command shows memory and CPU statistics refreshed every 2 seconds?
explanation: vmstat 2 prints memory, swap, I/O and CPU statistics every 2 seconds until stopped. free -h prints once, and uptime shows load average.

scenario: Which tool creates GPT partitions non-interactively with a single command?

options.text: parted (for example parted /dev/vdb mkpart data xfs 1MiB 1GiB)

explanation: parted configures GPT partitions non-interactively: parted /dev/vdb mklabel gpt, then mkpart. fdisk and gdisk are interactive. Run partprobe or udevadm settle if the kernel doesn't see the new partition.

scenario: Which commands create a 2 GiB logical volume named lvdata in a new volume group vgdata on /dev/vdb1?

options.text: pvcreate /dev/vdb1; vgcreate vgdata /dev/vdb1; lvcreate -n lvdata -L 2G vgdata

options.note: Needs a VG name, not a partition.

explanation: Build the stack in order: pvcreate /dev/vdb1, vgcreate vgdata /dev/vdb1, then lvcreate -n lvdata -L 2G vgdata. The volume appears as /dev/vgdata/lvdata and /dev/mapper/vgdata-lvdata.

refs.title: Configuring and managing logical volumes - RHEL 9

scenario: Create a logical volume of exactly 50 extents in vgapp, where each extent is 16 MiB. Which command?

options.note: -L means size in MiB by default (50 MiB).

explanation: lvcreate -l 50 allocates 50 extents (-L would mean a size), and extent size is set when creating the VG: vgcreate -s 16M. -l 100%FREE uses all free space.

scenario: How do you add the new partition /dev/vdc1 to the existing volume group vgdata?
explanation: Initialize the partition with pvcreate, then vgextend vgdata /dev/vdc1 adds it to the volume group; verify with pvs and vgs. lvextend grows a logical volume, not a VG.

refs.title: Configuring and managing logical volumes - RHEL 9

scenario: Which /etc/fstab line activates a swap logical volume at boot?
explanation: A swap LV needs mkswap and the fstab line /dev/vgdata/lvswap none swap defaults 0 0; test with swapon -a and check swapon --show. Swap has no mount point, so the mount field is 'none'.

scenario: You need more swap without touching existing data. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Create a new partition or LV, run mkswap on it, add it to /etc/fstab, and swapon -a
Resize the existing swap while in use

explanation: To add swap safely, use a new partition or LV, run mkswap, add it to /etc/fstab and run swapon -a. Never reuse a partition holding data, and swap can't be resized while in use.

scenario: Which command shows UUIDs and file system types of block devices?
explanation: blkid (or lsblk -f) shows UUIDs, labels and file system types. Use UUID= or LABEL= in fstab so mounts survive device-name changes.

scenario: Which command assigns the label DATA to an XFS file system on /dev/vdb1?

options.note: e2label is for ext file systems.

explanation: xfs_admin -L DATA /dev/vdb1 sets the label on an unmounted XFS file system, and you can also set it at creation with mkfs.xfs -L. e2label is for ext file systems.

scenario: What does vgdisplay vgdata show that helps size a new logical volume?

options.text: The physical extent size and the number of free extents

explanation: vgdisplay shows the physical extent (PE) size and free PE count; free space is free PE times PE size, which tells you how large a new logical volume can be.

refs.title: Configuring and managing logical volumes - RHEL 9

scenario: After creating a partition, lsblk doesn't show it. What should you run?
explanation: partprobe /dev/vdb (or udevadm settle) makes the kernel reread the partition table so lsblk shows the new partition. A reboot also works but is rarely needed.

scenario: Which GPT partition type is appropriate for a partition you'll add to LVM?

options.text: Linux LVM (set with parted set N lvm on)

explanation: Mark an LVM partition with the 'Linux LVM' type (parted set N lvm on). pvcreate works without the flag, but it documents intent; EFI System and BIOS boot are for other uses.

scenario: Which command creates an XFS file system on /dev/vgdata/lvdata?

options.note: Points at the VG, not the LV.

explanation: mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvdata creates an XFS file system on the logical volume. xfs_growfs resizes an existing one and mkfs.ext4 makes ext4.

scenario: Mount /dev/vgdata/lvdata at /data persistently. Which steps are complete and safe?

options.text: mkdir /data; add a UUID=... /data xfs defaults 0 0 line to /etc/fstab; systemctl daemon-reload; mount -a
Add the line and reboot without testing

explanation: To mount persistently: create the mount point, add a UUID=... /data xfs defaults 0 0 line to /etc/fstab, run systemctl daemon-reload and mount -a. Testing with mount -a avoids an unbootable system, and findmnt verifies the result.

scenario: Grow the XFS logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvdata to 3 GiB total while it stays mounted. Which command?

options.note: Adds 3 GiB instead of setting 3 GiB, and doesn't grow XFS.
resize2fs is for ext file systems.

explanation: lvextend -r -L 3G sets the LV to 3 GiB total and -r grows the file system too (xfs_growfs for XFS) while mounted. Without -r you must run xfs_growfs /data yourself, and resize2fs is for ext4.

scenario: The task says a logical volume must be resized to a size between 830 MiB and 890 MiB. What should you aim for?

options.text: A value safely inside the range, such as 850M, then verify with lvs and df -h

options.note: Rounding to extents may land outside the range.

explanation: When a size range is given, choose a value safely inside it, such as 850M. Sizes round to whole extents, so exact edge values can land outside the range. Verify with lvs and df -h.

scenario: Which /etc/fstab line mounts the NFS export server1:/exports/data at /mnt/data?
explanation: An NFS fstab entry lists server:/export first, then the mount point, type nfs and options including _netdev. showmount -e server1 lists exports, and nfs-utils may need installing.

scenario: Users' home directories on nfs.example.com:/home/guests/<user> must mount automatically at /home/guests/<user> when accessed. Which approach fits?

options.text: autofs: a master map entry /home/guests /etc/auto.guests and a wildcard map * -rw,sync nfs.example.com:/home/guests/&
A separate fstab line per user
options.note: Doesn't scale and mounts everything at boot.

options.text: A cron job that mounts every minute
Symbolic links to the NFS server

explanation: autofs mounts on demand: a master map entry (/home/guests /etc/auto.guests) and a wildcard map (* -rw,sync nfs.example.com:/home/guests/&) mount each user's home when accessed. Install autofs and enable --now; per-user fstab lines mount everything at boot.

scenario: Which command mounts a FAT USB drive at /mnt/usb?

options.note: Wrong type and no mount point.

explanation: mount -t vfat /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb mounts a FAT drive. VFAT has no Unix permissions, so control access with uid=, gid= and umask= mount options.

scenario: A user in the group "projects" can't create files in /srv/projects (mode 755, root:projects). What minimal change fixes it?

options.note: Takes it away from the team.

explanation: The group needs write permission on the directory, so chmod 775 (g+w) fixes it with minimal change; 777 is too open. Add g+s so new files keep the projects group.

scenario: Which command gives user jlee read and write access to /srv/reports/q3.xlsx with an ACL?
explanation: setfacl -m u:jlee:rw file grants jlee read/write without changing owner, group or mode; getfacl shows ACLs. Effective rights are limited by the ACL mask.

scenario: Which command shows mounted file systems in a tree with their options?
explanation: findmnt shows mounted file systems as a tree with options; findmnt /data checks one mount point and findmnt --verify checks fstab syntax.

scenario: What happens if an /etc/fstab entry for a missing device has no nofail option?

options.text: Boot waits and then drops to emergency mode

explanation: Without nofail, a missing device makes the boot wait and then drop to emergency mode. Use nofail for removable or optional storage.

scenario: Configure the system to use the repository at http://content.example.com/rhel10/BaseOS. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Create a .repo file in /etc/yum.repos.d with a [BaseOS] section, baseurl=http://content.example.com/rhel10/BaseOS, enabled=1, and gpgcheck settings

options.note: Needs a repo section and the full URL, usually in /etc/yum.repos.d.

options.text: Use the keys url= and on=1 in the repo file
options.note: The keys are baseurl= and enabled=.

explanation: Define the repository in a .repo file under /etc/yum.repos.d with a [BaseOS] section containing name, baseurl=, enabled=1 and gpgcheck settings (or use dnf config-manager --add-repo). Check with dnf repolist. dnf.conf isn't where repos are defined.

refs.title: Managing software with the DNF tool - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command installs the httpd package and answers yes automatically?

options.note: Needs a package file and doesn't resolve dependencies.

explanation: dnf install -y httpd installs the package and answers yes to prompts. rpm -i doesn't resolve dependencies.

refs.title: Managing software with the DNF tool - RHEL 9

scenario: Which commands add the Flathub remote and install an app from it with Flatpak?

options.text: flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo, then flatpak install flathub <app-id>

explanation: Add the remote with flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub <flatpakrepo URL> and then flatpak install flathub <app-id>. flatpak list shows installed apps, and dnf is for RPM packages.

scenario: Which crontab entry for user natasha runs /usr/bin/logger "hello" every 5 minutes?

options.note: Runs at minute 5 of every hour.
Every minute of every fifth hour.

explanation: */5 * * * * runs every five minutes (the minute field uses step syntax), and the user can be set with crontab -e -u natasha. A leading 5 would run only at minute 5, and six fields is invalid.

scenario: Which pair of systemd units runs a job daily, catching up if the system was off?

options.text: backup.service plus backup.timer with OnCalendar=daily and Persistent=true

explanation: Pair backup.service with backup.timer using OnCalendar=daily and Persistent=true so missed runs are caught up; enable the timer (systemctl enable --now backup.timer), not the service. systemctl list-timers shows them.

scenario: Which command schedules a one-time job to run in 10 minutes?
explanation: echo "script" | at now + 10 minutes schedules a one-time job; atd must be running. atq lists jobs and atrm removes them. cron is for repeating jobs.

scenario: Configure the system as an NTP client of classroom.example.com. What do you do?

options.text: Add server classroom.example.com iburst to /etc/chrony.conf, restart chronyd, and check with chronyc sources

explanation: Add 'server classroom.example.com iburst' to /etc/chrony.conf, restart chronyd and check chronyc sources. RHEL uses chrony, not ntpd, and timedatectl set-ntp only toggles synchronization.

scenario: Which command makes the system boot a specific installed kernel by default?
explanation: grubby --set-default /boot/vmlinuz-<version> sets the default boot kernel; grubby --default-kernel shows it. There is no dnf option for this.

refs.title: Managing, monitoring, and updating the kernel - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command adds a kernel argument to all installed kernels on RHEL?

options.note: sysctl is for runtime kernel parameters, not boot args.

explanation: grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="audit=1" adds a kernel argument to every installed kernel. The alternative is editing GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub and regenerating with grub2-mkconfig; editing grub.cfg directly gets overwritten.

refs.title: Managing, monitoring, and updating the kernel - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command updates all packages to their latest available versions?
explanation: dnf upgrade (or dnf update) updates all packages to the latest available versions. Kernel updates install alongside the old kernel, so you can fall back.

refs.title: Managing software with the DNF tool - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command installs a local RPM file and resolves its dependencies from enabled repositories?
explanation: dnf install ./package.rpm installs a local RPM and resolves dependencies from enabled repositories. rpm -i does not fetch dependencies, and rpm -qip shows package information.

refs.title: Managing software with the DNF tool - RHEL 9

scenario: Which command makes the httpd service start automatically at boot without starting it now?
explanation: systemctl enable httpd creates the boot-time symlink without starting the service; enable --now does both. Graders often reboot, so a service must be enabled as well as running.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: Which command sets the time zone to Europe/London?
explanation: timedatectl set-timezone Europe/London sets the system time zone; timedatectl list-timezones lists valid names. Exporting TZ only affects the current shell.

scenario: Set a static IPv4 address 172.25.250.11/24, gateway 172.25.250.254, and DNS 172.25.250.254 on connection "eth0". Which command does it persistently?

options.text: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.11/24 ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 ipv4.dns 172.25.250.254 ipv4.method manual, then nmcli con up eth0

options.note: RHEL 10 uses NetworkManager keyfiles; ifcfg is no longer used.

explanation: nmcli con mod sets the static address, gateway, DNS and ipv4.method manual persistently, and nmcli con up applies it. ip addr add and ifconfig are temporary; ifcfg files are the legacy format, as profiles now live in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections.

scenario: Add a static IPv6 address fd00::11/64 to connection eth0 without removing IPv4.

options.text: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00::11/64 ipv6.method manual; nmcli con up eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses fd00::11/64
ip -6 addr add fd00::11/64 dev eth0 only

explanation: Add an IPv6 address with nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00::11/64 ipv6.method manual and activate the connection; IPv4 settings stay as they were. Use +ipv6.addresses to add rather than replace, and verify with ip -6 addr.

scenario: Which command sets the hostname to servera.lab.example.com persistently?
explanation: hostnamectl set-hostname servera.lab.example.com makes the name persistent by writing /etc/hostname. The plain hostname command changes it only until reboot.

scenario: Which file resolves a host name without DNS?
explanation: /etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses locally, without DNS; lines are IP name aliases. /etc/resolv.conf lists DNS servers.

scenario: Which command shows whether connection eth0 starts automatically at boot?
explanation: nmcli -g connection.autoconnect con show eth0 shows whether the profile starts automatically; set it with nmcli con mod eth0 connection.autoconnect yes.

scenario: Which command confirms DNS resolution of utility.lab.example.com?

options.text: host utility.lab.example.com (or dig, or getent hosts)

explanation: host or dig test DNS resolution directly, and getent hosts follows /etc/nsswitch.conf including /etc/hosts. ping tests reachability, not the DNS answer itself.

scenario: Which command shows the routing table?
explanation: ip route shows the routing table; the default route appears as 'default via <gateway> dev <iface>'. ip addr shows addresses.

scenario: Which command shows which ports sshd and httpd are listening on?
explanation: ss -tlnp lists listening TCP sockets with numeric ports and the owning process, which tells you the address and port each service listens on when it isn't reachable.

scenario: Create a group sysadms and user harry with supplementary group sysadms. Which commands?

options.text: usermod -G sysadms harry before creating him

explanation: Create the group first (groupadd sysadms) and then the user with supplementary group: useradd -G sysadms harry. Lowercase -g sets the primary group instead. Set the password with passwd --stdin.

scenario: Create user sarah with UID 3533 and no interactive shell.
explanation: useradd -u 3533 -s /sbin/nologin sarah sets the UID and denies interactive login. Verify with id sarah or grep sarah /etc/passwd.

scenario: All new users must have passwords that expire after 90 days. What do you change?
explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS 90 in /etc/login.defs applies to accounts created afterward. For existing users run chage -M 90 user.

scenario: User natasha's password must expire every 30 days. Which command?
explanation: chage -M 30 natasha sets the maximum password age to 30 days; -E sets the account expiry date instead. chage -l shows aging and chage -d 0 forces a change at next login.

scenario: Members of group sysadms should run any command with sudo. What is the cleanest configuration?

options.text: Create /etc/sudoers.d/sysadms containing %sysadms ALL=(ALL) ALL (edit with visudo -f)
Add them to the root group

explanation: Create /etc/sudoers.d/sysadms containing %sysadms ALL=(ALL) ALL using visudo -f, which checks syntax. Don't loosen /etc/sudoers permissions or share root's password; members of wheel already have full sudo on RHEL.

scenario: Which command adds harry to the wheel group without removing his other supplementary groups?

options.note: Wrong syntax; gpasswd -a harry wheel works.

explanation: usermod -aG wheel harry appends the group and keeps his other supplementary groups; without -a the -G option replaces them. gpasswd -a is an alternative.

scenario: Which command deletes user tom and his home directory and mail spool?
explanation: userdel -r tom deletes the user and removes the home directory and mail spool. Without -r the home stays; check for leftover files with find / -nouser.

scenario: Which command shows a user's UID, primary group, and supplementary groups?
explanation: id username shows the UID, primary group and supplementary groups; getent passwd username shows the account line. who shows logged-in users.

scenario: Allow HTTP through the firewall now and after reboot. Which commands?
explanation: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http saves the rule and --reload applies it, so it works now and after reboot. Without --permanent it's lost on reload; iptables rules aren't how firewalld is managed.

refs.title: Configuring firewalls and packet filters - RHEL 9

scenario: Open TCP port 82 in the firewall permanently.
explanation: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=82/tcp followed by --reload opens TCP port 82 persistently. --add-service takes a service name, not a number, and semanage port is SELinux labeling.

refs.title: Configuring firewalls and packet filters - RHEL 9

scenario: httpd must listen on port 82, and SELinux is enforcing. Besides Listen 82 in httpd.conf, which SELinux command is required?

options.note: Disables protection rather than fixing the label.

explanation: SELinux only lets httpd bind labeled ports, so besides Listen 82 label the port: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 82. Then restart httpd and open the port in firewalld. Disabling SELinux is not the fix.

scenario: Web content was moved to /srv/web. Which commands label it for httpd so the label survives a relabel?

options.note: Temporary: a relabel or restorecon reverts it.
Booleans toggle policy features; they don't label files.

explanation: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' records the labeling rule, and restorecon -Rv applies it, so it survives a relabel. chcon alone is lost on relabel.

scenario: Which command shows the current SELinux mode?
explanation: getenforce prints the current SELinux mode; sestatus gives mode, policy and the configured mode. setenforce changes the mode.

scenario: The system must boot in enforcing mode. Where is that set?
explanation: SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config makes enforcing the boot default; setenforce 1 only lasts until reboot. Moving from disabled to enforcing triggers a relabel at boot.

scenario: Which command permanently allows httpd to connect to remote databases?
explanation: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on persistently allows httpd to connect to remote databases; without -P it reverts at reboot. getsebool -a lists booleans.

scenario: How do you find recent SELinux denials?
explanation: ausearch -m AVC -ts recent shows recent SELinux denials from /var/log/audit/audit.log, and sealert (setroubleshoot) suggests fixes.

scenario: Which command shows the SELinux context of running httpd processes?
explanation: ps -eZ | grep httpd shows the SELinux context of running processes; httpd runs in the httpd_t domain. ls -Z shows file contexts instead.

scenario: A file copied from /root into /var/www/html keeps admin_home_t and httpd can't read it. What is the quickest correct fix?
explanation: A file copied from /root may keep admin_home_t if it was moved; restorecon -v resets it to the default context for its new location. cp usually takes the destination's default context but mv keeps the original.

scenario: Configure key-based SSH so root on servera can log in to serverb as student without a password. Which steps?

options.text: ssh-keygen on servera, then ssh-copy-id student@serverb

explanation: Run ssh-keygen on servera and ssh-copy-id student@serverb to place the public key in ~student/.ssh/authorized_keys on serverb (mode 600 in a 700 .ssh directory). Never copy the private key or allow empty passwords.

scenario: Every new file created by user student should be mode 640 and every new directory 750. Which umask?

options.note: That's a mode, not a umask.

explanation: umask 027 removes group write and all other permissions: files get 640 and directories 750. Set it in ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile for the user, or system-wide in /etc/profile.d or /etc/login.defs.

scenario: Which SELinux mode logs denials without blocking them?

options.note: The policy type, not a mode.

explanation: Permissive mode logs SELinux denials without blocking them, useful briefly for troubleshooting; enforcing blocks, and disabled turns SELinux off. Targeted is a policy type, not a mode.
